entries.dd3bd3fd36f4a63258177e51da8ea37769b47278: <div sID="gen12279" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="100" osisID="Ps.100" sID="Ps.100"/> <div eID="gen12279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12280" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12281" type="x-p"/> It is with good reason that many sing this psalm very frequently in their religious assemblies, for it is very proper both to express and to excite pious and devout affections towards God in our approach to him in holy ordinances; and, if our hearts go along with the words, we shall make melody in it to the Lord. The Jews say it was penned to be sung with their thank-offerings; perhaps it was; but we say that as there is nothing in it peculiar to their economy so its beginning with a call to all lands to praise God plainly extends it to the gospel-church. Here, I. We are called upon to praise God and rejoice in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.1-Ps.100.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.4">4</reference>. II. We are furnished with matter for praise; we must praise him, considering his being and relation to us (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">ver. 3</reference>) and his mercy and truth, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.5">ver. 5</reference>. These are plain and common things, and therefore the more fit to be the matter of devotion.
entries.461d09e3036871efd5085a133dad4ffbb2820f7c: <div eID="gen12281" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12280" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Importunate Exhortations to Praise God; Motives for Praising God.</title> <div sID="gen12282" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Make a joyful noise unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all ye lands. <hi type="super">2</hi> Serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with gladness: come before his presence with singing. <hi type="super">3</hi> Know ye that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> God: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> he <hi type="italic">that</hi> hath made us, and not we ourselves; <hi type="italic">we are</hi> his people, and the sheep of his pasture. <hi type="super">4</hi> Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, <hi type="italic">and</hi> into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bless his name. <hi type="super">5</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good; his mercy <hi type="italic">is</hi> everlasting; and his truth <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> to all generations. <div eID="gen12282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12283" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The exhortations to praise are very importunate. The psalm does indeed answer to the title, <hi type="italic">A psalm of praise;</hi> it begins with that call which of late we have several times met with (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all you lands,</hi> or <hi type="italic">all the earth,</hi> all the inhabitants of the earth. When all nations shall be discipled, and the gospel preached to every creature, then this summons will be fully answered to. But, if we take the foregoing psalm to be (as we have opened it) a call to the Jewish church to rejoice in the administration of God's kingdom, which they were under (as the four psalms before it were calculated for the days of the Messiah), this psalm, perhaps, was intended for proselytes, that came over out of all lands to the Jews' religion. However, we have here, 1. A strong invitation to worship God; not that God needs us, or any thing we have or can do, but it is his will that we should <hi type="italic">serve the Lord,</hi> should devote ourselves to his service and employ ourselves in it; and that we should not only serve him in all instances of obedience to his law, but that we should <hi type="italic">come before his presence</hi> in the ordinances which he has appointed and in which he has promised to manifest himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.2">v. 2</reference>), that we should <hi type="italic">enter into his gates and into his courts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.4">v. 4</reference>), that we should attend upon him among his servants, and keep there where he keeps court. In all acts of religious worship, whether in secret or in our families, we come into God's presence, and serve him; but it is in public worship especially that we <hi type="italic">enter into his gates and into his courts.</hi> The people were not permitted to enter into the holy place; there the priests only went in to minister. But let the people be thankful for their place in the courts of God's house, to which they were admitted and where they gave their attendance. 2. Great encouragement given us, in worshipping God, to do it cheerfully (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Serve the Lord with gladness.</hi> This intimates a prediction that in gospel-times there should be special occasion for joy; and it prescribes this as a rule of worship: Let God be <hi type="italic">served with gladness.</hi> By holy joy we do really serve God; it is an honour to him to rejoice in him; and we ought to serve him with holy joy. Gospel-worshippers should be joyful worshippers; if we serve God in uprightness, let us serve him with gladness. We must be willing and forward to it, glad when we are called to <hi type="italic">go up to the house of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.1">Ps. cxxii. 1</reference>), looking upon it as the comfort of our lives to have communion with God; and we must be pleasant and cheerful in it, must say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here,</hi> approaching to God, in every duty, as <hi type="italic">to God our exceeding Joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Ps. xliii. 4</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">come before his presence with singing,</hi> not only songs of joy, but songs of praise. <hi type="italic">Enter into his gates with thanksgiving,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.100.4">v. 4</reference>. We must not only comfort ourselves, but glorify God, with our joy, and let him have the praise of that which we have the pleasure of. <hi type="italic">Be thankful to him and bless his name;</hi> that is, (1.) We must take it as a favour to be admitted into his service, and give him thanks that we have liberty of access to him, that we have ordinances instituted and opportunity continued of waiting upon God in those ordinances. (2.) We must intermix praise and thanksgiving with all our services. This golden thread must run through every duty (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), for it is the work of angels. <hi type="italic">In every thing give thanks,</hi> in every ordinance, as well as in every providence. <div eID="gen12283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12284" type="x-p"/> II. The matter of praise, and motives to it, are very important, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.100.5">5</reference>. Know you what God is in himself and what he is to you. Note, Knowledge is the mother of devotion and of all obedience: blind sacrifices will never please a seeing God. "Know it; consider and apply it, and then you will be more close and constant, more inward and serious, in the worship of him." Let us know then these seven things concerning the Lord Jehovah, with whom we have to do in all the acts of religious worship:—1. <hi type="italic">That the Lord he is God,</hi> the only living and true God—that he is a Being infinitely perfect, self-existent, and self-sufficient, and the fountain of all being; he is God, and not a man as we are. He is an eternal Spirit, incomprehensible and independent, the first cause and last end. The heathen worshipped the creature of their own fancy; the workmen made it, therefore it is not God. We worship him that made us and all the world; he is God, and all other pretended deities are vanity and a lie, and such as he has triumphed over. 2. That he is our Creator: <hi type="italic">It is he that has made us, and not we ourselves.</hi> I find that I am, but cannot say, <hi type="italic">I am that I am,</hi> and therefore must ask, Whence am I? Who made me? <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker?</hi> And it is the Lord Jehovah. He gave us being, he gave us this being; he is both the former of our bodies and the Father of our spirits. We did not, we could not, make ourselves. It is God's prerogative to be his own cause; our being is derived and depending. 3. That therefore he is our rightful owner. The Masorites, by altering one letter in the Hebrew, read it, <hi type="italic">He made us, and his we are,</hi> or <hi type="italic">to him we belong.</hi> Put both the readings together, and we learn that because God <hi type="italic">made us, and not we ourselves,</hi> therefore we are not our own, but his. He has an incontestable right to, and property in, us and all things. His we are, to be actuated by his power, disposed of by his will, and devoted to his honour and glory. 4. That he is our sovereign ruler: <hi type="italic">We are his people</hi> or subjects, and he is our prince, our rector or governor, that gives law to us as moral agents, and will call us to an account for what we do. <hi type="italic">The Lord is our judge; the Lord is our lawgiver.</hi> We are not at liberty to do what we will, but must always make conscience of doing as we are bidden. 5. That he is our bountiful benefactor. We are not only his sheep, whom he is entitled to, but <hi type="italic">the sheep of his pasture,</hi> whom he takes care of; the <hi type="italic">flock of his feeding</hi> (so it may be read); therefore the <hi type="italic">sheep of his hand;</hi> at his disposal because <hi type="italic">the sheep of his pasture,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">Ps. xcv. 7</reference>. He that made us maintains us, and gives us all good things richly to enjoy. 6. That he is a God of infinite mercy and goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is good,</hi> and therefore does good; <hi type="italic">his mercy is everlasting;</hi> it is a fountain that can never be drawn dry. The saints, who are now the sanctified vessels of mercy, will be, to eternity, the glorified monuments of mercy. 7. That he is a God of inviolable truth and faithfulness: <hi type="italic">His truth endures to all generations,</hi> and no word of his shall fall to the ground as antiquated or revoked. The promise is sure to all the seed, from age to age.  <chapter eID="Ps.100"/> <div eID="gen12284" type="x-p"/>

entries.91fa4ff6bdc4d37dad7b1b66fff0a5e8884c351d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6643"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 100</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5">Psa 100:1-5</reference>. As closing this series (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>), this Psalm is a general call on all the earth to render exalted praise to God, the creator, preserver, and benefactor of men.</title> <div sID="gen10174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6643"/>1-2. With thankful praise, unite service as the subjects of a king (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">Psa 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen10174" type="x-p"/>
entries.89463b6e80570826cdc2faaa217ac9920346de5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6644"/><div sID="gen10175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6644"/>3. To the obligations of a creature and subject is added that of a beneficiary (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10175" type="x-p"/>
entries.f165cf0125d9d77e03d8486e48115b55547bfa2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6645"/><div sID="gen10176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6645"/>4. Join joyfully in His public worship. The terms are, of course, figurative (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">92:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Is 66:23</reference>).<div eID="gen10176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Enter--</hi>or, "Come with solemnity" (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.6">Psa 95:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10177" type="x-p"/>
entries.9802c26d08d0cb2f3d15eb9dd7b1d84a0f996e89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6646"/><div sID="gen10178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6646"/>5. The reason: God's eternal mercy and truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">Psa 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">89:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.100"/>

entries.37ffc47ce2e71c222dc0cb69688bacbbb81fc86e: <div eID="gen21913" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21914" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21914" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> All nations are exhorted to praise the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1">Psa 100:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.2">Psa 100:2</reference>; to acknowledge him to be the Sovereign God and their Creator and that they are his people and the flock of his pasture, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>; to worship him publicly, and be grateful for his mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.4">Psa 100:4</reference>. The reasons on which this is founded; his own goodness, his everlasting mercy, and his ever-during truth, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.5">Psa 100:5</reference>. <div eID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is entitled in the Hebrew מזמור לתודה mizmor lethodah, not "A Psalm of Praise," as we have it, but "A Psalm for the confession, or for the confession-offering," very properly translated by the Chaldee: שבחא על קורבן תודתא shibcha al kurban todetha, "Praise for the sacrifice (or offering) of confession." The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Ethiopic have followed this sense. The Arabic attributes it to David. The Syriac has the following prefixed: "Without a name. Concerning Joshua the son of Nun, when he had ended the war with the Ammonites: but in the new covenant it relates to the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith." It is likely that it was composed after the captivity, as a form of thanksgiving to God for that great deliverance, as well as an inducement to the people to consecrate themselves to him, and to be exact in the performance of the acts of public worship. <div eID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> Make a joyful noise - הריעו hariu, exult, triumph, leap for joy. <div eID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> All ye lands - Not only Jews, but Gentiles, for the Lord bestows his benefits on all with a liberal hand.
entries.c90be9a5edeb4f023d95d57bbe5317b3b121f9ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> Serve the Lord with gladness - It is your privilege and duty to be happy in your religious worship. The religion of the true God is intended to remove human misery, and to make mankind happy. He whom the religion of Christ has not made happy does not understand that religion, or does not make a proper use of it.
entries.b6cfa0b4c5f7588af46f15bd58e2d3e32ee95a12: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> Know ye that the Lord he is God - Acknowledge in every possible way, both in public and private, that Jehovah, the uncreated self-existent, and eternal Being, is Elohim, the God who is in covenant with man, to instruct, redeem, love, and make him finally happy. <div eID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> It is he that hath made us - He is our Creator and has consequently the only right in and over us. <div eID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> And not we ourselves - ולא אנחנו velo anachnu. I can never think that this is the true reading, though found in the present Hebrew text, in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Syriac. Was there ever a people on earth, however grossly heathenish, that did believe, or could believe, that they had made themselves? In twenty-six of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. we have ולו אנחנו velo anachnu, "and His we are;" לו lo, the pronoun, being put for לא lo, the negative particle. This is the reading of the Targum, or Chaldee paraphrase ודיליה אנחנא vedileyh anachna, "and his we are," and is the reading of the text in the Complutensian Polyglot, of both the Psalters which were printed in 1477, and is the keri, or marginal reading in most Masoretic Bibles. Every person must see, from the nature of the subject that it is the genuine reading. The position is founded on the maxim that what a man invents, constructs out of his own matterials, without assistance in genius, materials or execution from any other person, is His Own and to it, its use, and produce, he has the only right. God made us, therefore we are His: we are his people, and should acknowledge him for our God; we are the sheep of his pasture, and should devote the lives to him constantly which he continually supports.
entries.8fa02c4ef90f42e60bb23c6e4e0ba4e6528f894f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> Enter into his gates with thanksgiving - Publicly worship God; and when ye come to the house of prayer, be thankful that you have such a privilege; and when you enter his courts, praise him for the permission. <div eID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> The word בתודה bethodah, which we render with thanksgiving, is properly with the confession-offering or sacrifice. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1-Psa.100.5">Psa 100:1-5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> Bless his name - Bless Jehovah, that he is your Elohim; see <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>. In our liturgic service we say, "Speak good of his name;" we cannot do otherwise; we have nothing but good to speak of our God.
entries.f81b779b35f9d5d6f8b86a6c028de9b899391161: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> For the Lord is good - Goodness the perfect, eternal opposition to all badness and evil, is essential to God. Mercy and compassion are modifications of his goodness; and as his nature is eternal, so his mercy, springing from his goodness, must be everlasting. And as Truth is an essential characteristic of an infinitely intelligent and perfect nature; therefore God's truth must endure from generation to generation. Whatsoever he has promised must be fulfilled, through all the successive generations of men, as long as sun and moon shall last. <div eID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> As this is a very important Psalm, and has long made a part of our public worship, I shall lay it before the reader in the oldest vernacular Versions I have hitherto met with, - the Anglo-Saxon and the Anglo-Scottish, with a literal interlineary translation of the former. <div eID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> The Anglo-Saxon Hundredth Psalm <div eID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> Rhyme ye the Lord all earth, serve the Lord in bliss; <div eID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> Infare in sight his in blithness; <div eID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> Wit ye, for that Lord he is God, he did us &not self we; <div eID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> Folk his &sheep leeseway his; fare into gates his in confession, into courts is in hymns confess him. <div eID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> Praise name his, for that winsom is; Lord thro' eternity mildheartedness his, &unto on kindred &kindred sothfastnes his <div eID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> The reader will see that, in order to make this translation as literal as possible, I have preserved some old English words which we had from the Anglo-Saxon, and which have nearly become obsolete: e.g., Infare, "to go in;" blithness, "joy, exultation;" twit ye, "know ye;" did, the preterite of to do, "made, created," the literal translation of the Hebrew, עשה asah, he made; leeseway, "pasturage on a common;" winsom, "cheerful, merry;" mildheartedness, "tenderness of heart, compassion;" sothfastness, "steady to the sooth or truth, fast to truth." I might have noticed some various readings in Anglo-Saxon MSS.; e.g., <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1">Psa 100:1</reference> for idrymeth, "rhyme ye;" winsumiath, "be winsom, be joyful." And <reference osisRef="Psa.100.5">Psa 100:5</reference>, for winsom, "cheerful;" swete, "sweet." <div eID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> Anglo-Scottish Version of the Hundredth Psalm <div eID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21938" type="x-p"/> 1. Joyes to God al the erth; serves to Lord in gladnes. <div eID="gen21938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21939" type="x-p"/> 2. Enters in his sight with joying. <div eID="gen21939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> 3. Wittes for Lorde he is God; he made us and noght we; <div eID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> 4. Folke of hym, and schepe of his pasture; enters the gates of hym in schrift; hys Halles in ympnys; schryves to hym. <div eID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> 5. Loues his name, for soft is Lorde; withouten end in his mercy; and in generation and generation the sothfastnes of hym. <div eID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21943" type="x-p"/> Thus our forefathers said and sung in heart and mouth and with their tongues made confession to salvation. There are but few words here which require explanation: <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>, Wittes, "wot ye, know ye." <reference osisRef="Psa.100.4">Psa 100:4</reference>, Schrift, "confession;" schryves, "confess ye." <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi>, Loues, "praise ye, laud ye." Sothfastness, as above, steadfastness in the truth.  <chapter eID="Ps.100"/> <div eID="gen21943" type="x-p"/>

entries.0564cadcc7b744ff69105d0efc3cc11eb2bdfa8d: <div eID="gen9968" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Call of All the World to the Service of the True God</title> <div sID="gen9969" type="x-p"/> This Psalm closes the series of deutero-Isaianic Psalms, which began with Ps 91. There is common to all of them that mild sublimity, sunny cheerfulness, unsorrowful spiritual character, and New Testament expandedness, which we wonder at in the second part of the Book of Isaiah; and besides all this, they are also linked together by the figure anadiplosis, and manifold consonances and accords. <div eID="gen9969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9970" type="x-p"/> The arrangement, too, at least from <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference> onwards, is Isaianic: it is parallel with the relation of <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Isa 24:1</reference> to Psa 13:1. Just as the former cycle of prophecies closes that concerning the nations, after the manner of a musical finale, so the Psalms celebrating the dominion of God, from <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference> onwards, which vividly portray the unfolded glory of the kingship of Jahve, have <hi type="italic">Jubilate</hi> and <hi type="italic">Cantate</hi> Psalms in succession. <div eID="gen9970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9971" type="x-p"/> From the fact that this last Jubilate is entirely the echo of the first, viz., of the first half of <reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11">Psa 95:1-11</reference>, we see how ingenious the arrangement is. There we find all the thoughts which recur here. There it is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>, <hi type="italic">He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture and the flock of His hand.</hi> And in <reference osisRef="Ps.95.2">Psa 95:2</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let us come before His face with thanksgiving</hi> (בּתודה), <hi type="italic">let us make a joyful noise unto Him in songs!</hi> <div eID="gen9971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9972" type="x-p"/> This תודה is found here in the title of the Psalm, מזמור לתּודה. Taken in the sense of a “Psalm for thanksgiving,” it would say but little. We may take לתודה in a liturgical sense (with the Targum, Mendelssohn, Ewald, and Hitzig), like ליום השׁבת, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.1">Psa 92:1</reference>, in this series, and like להזכיר in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">Psa 38:1</reference>; Psa 70:1. What is intended is not merely the <hi type="italic">tôda</hi> of the heart, but the <hi type="italic">shelamı̂m - tôda</hi>, תּודה זבח, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.22">Psa 107:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">Psa 116:17</reference>, which is also called absolutely תודה in <reference osisRef="Ps.56.13">Psa 56:13</reference>, 2Ch 29:31. That kind of <hi type="italic">shelamı̂m</hi> is thus called which is presented על־תודה, i.e., as thankful praise for divine benefits received, more particularly marvellous protection and deliverance (vid., Ps 107).
entries.fe65f3905adedca43fc32e3d37c4e46e27cec4c5: <reference osisRef="Ps.100.1-Ps.100.3">Psa 100:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9973" type="x-p"/> The call in <reference osisRef="Ps.100.1">Psa 100:1</reference> sounds like <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">Psa 98:4</reference>; Psa 66:1. כּל־הארץ are all lands, or rather all men belonging to the earth’s population. The first verse, without any parallelism and in so far monostichic, is like the signal for a blowing of the trumpets. Instead of “serve Jahve with gladness (בּשׂמחה),” it is expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">Psa 2:11</reference>, “serve Jahve with fear (בּיראה).” Fear and joy do not exclude one another. Fear becomes the exalted Lord, and the holy gravity of His requirements; joy becomes the gracious Lord, and His blessed service. The summons to manifest this joy in a religious, festive manner springs up out of an all-hopeful, world-embracing love, and this love is the spontaneous result of living faith in the promise that all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in the seed of Abraham, and in the prophecies in which this promise is unfolded. דּעוּ (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>) Theodoret well interprets δι ̓ αὐτῶν μάθετε τῶν πραγμάτων. They are to know from facts of outward and inward experience that Jahve is God: <hi type="italic">He hath made us, and not we ourselves</hi>. Thus runs the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, which the lxx follows, αὐτὸς ἔποήσεν ἡμᾶς καὶ οὐχ ἡμεῖς (as also the Syriac and Vulgate); but Symmachus (like Rashi), contrary to all possibilities of language, renders αὐτὸς ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς οὐκ ὄντας. Even the Midrash (<hi type="italic">Bereshith Rabba</hi>, ch. c. <hi type="italic">init</hi>.) finds in this confession the reverse of the arrogant words in the mouth of Pharaoh: “I myself have made myself” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, on the other hand, reads לו,<note placement="foot">According to the reckoning of the Masora, there are fifteen passages in the Old Testament in which לא is written and לו is read, viz., <reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.21">Lev 11:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.30">Lev 25:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.18">2Sa 16:18</reference>; 2Ki 8:10; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa 63:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference> cf. the note there, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.4">Psa 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.7">Pro 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.2">Pro 26:2</reference>; Ezr 4:2. Because doubtful, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa 49:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference> are not reckoned with these.</note> which the Targum, Jerome, and Saadia follow and render: <hi type="italic">et ipsius nos sumus</hi>. Hengstenberg calls this <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> quite unsuitable and bad; and Hupfeld, on the other hand, calls the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> an “unspeakable insipidity.” But in reality both readings accord with the context, and it is clear that they are both in harmony with Scripture. Many a one has drawn balsamic consolation from the words <hi type="italic">ipse fecit nos et non ipsi nos</hi>; e.g., Melancthon when disconsolately sorrowful over the body of his son in Dresden on the 12th July 1559. But in <hi type="italic">ipse fecit nos et ipsius nos sumus</hi> there is also a rich mine of comfort and of admonition, for the Creator of also the Owner, His heart clings to His creature, and the creature owes itself entirely to Him, without whom it would not have had a being, and would not continue in being. Since, however, the parallel passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>, favours ולו rather than ולא; since, further, ולא ,reh is the easier reading, inasmuch as הוּא leads one to expect that an antithesis will follow (Hitzig); and since the “His people and the sheep of His pasture” that follows is a more natural continuation of a preceding ולו אנחנו than that it should be attached as a predicative object to עשׂנוּ over a parenthetical ולא אנחנו: the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> decidedly maintains the preference. In connection with both readings, עשׂה has a sense related to the history of redemption, as in 1Sa 12:6. Israel is Jahve’s work (מעשׂה), <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">Isa 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Isa 60:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.6">Deu 32:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>, not merely as a people, but as the people of God, who were kept in view even in the calling of Abram.
entries.6b274002cee19c162f9caffb6e08f9f1516aa8de: <reference osisRef="Ps.100.4-Ps.100.5">Psa 100:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen9973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9974" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall the men of all nations enter with thanksgiving into the gates of His Temple and into the courts of His Temple with praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.8">Psa 96:8</reference>), in order to join themselves in worship to His church, which - a creation of Jahve for the good of the whole earth - is congregated about this Temple and has it as the place of its worship. The pilgrimage of all peoples to the holy mountain is an Old Testament dress of the hope for the conversion of all peoples to the God of revelation, and the close union of all with the people of this God. His Temple is open to them all. They may enter, and when they enter they have to look for great things. For the God of revelation (52:11; 54:8) is “good” (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">Psa 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.9">Psa 34:9</reference>), and His loving-kindness and faithfulness endure for ever - the thought that recurs frequently in the later Hallelujah and Hodu Psalms and is become a liturgical formula (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">Jer 33:11</reference>). The mercy of loving-kindness of God is the generosity, and His faithfulness the constancy, of His love.  <chapter eID="Ps.100"/> <div eID="gen9974" type="x-p"/>

entries.067780c6b0fd2966ea90c64391c5c80a88bd5b7f:
PSALM 100
The title of this psalm may serve for a summary of its contents Moreover, its brevity renders a lengthened discourse unnecessary. The Psalmist, in an especial manner, invites believers to praise God, because he has chosen them to be his people, and has taken them under his care.
Psalm 100:1-3
A Psalm of Praise
1. Let all the earth make a joyful noise to Jehovah. 2. Serve Jehovah with gladness: come into his presence with joyfulness. 3. Know ye that Jehovah himself is God: he made us, and not we ourselves: we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
 
1 Make a joyful noise The Psalmist refers only to that part of the service of God which consists in recounting his benefits and giving thanks. And since he invites the whole of the inhabitants of the earth indiscriminately to praise Jehovah, he seems, in the spirit of prophecy, to refer to the period when the Church would be gathered out of different nations. Hence he commands (verse 2) that God should be served with gladness, intimating that his kindness towards his own people is so great as to furnish them with abundant ground for rejoicing. This is better expressed in the third verse, in which he first reprehends the presumption of those men who had wickedly revolted from the true God, both in fashioning for themselves gods many, and in devising various forms of worshipping them. And as a multitude of gods destroys and suppresses the true knowledge of one God only, and tarnishes his glory, the prophet, with great propriety, calls upon all men to bethink themselves, and to cease from robbing God of the honor due to his name; and, at the same time, inveighs against their folly in that, not content with the one God, they were become vain in their imaginations. For, however much they are constrained to confess with the mouth that there is a God, the maker of heaven and earth, yet they are ever and anon gradually despoiling him of his glory; and in this manner, the Godhead is, to the utmost extent of their power, reduced to a nonentity. As it is then a most difficult thing to retain men in the practice of the pure worship of God, the prophet, not without reason, recalls the world from its accustomed vanity, and commands them to recognize God as God. For we must attend to this short definition of the knowledge of him, namely, that his glory be preserved unimpaired, and that no deity be opposed to him that might obscure the glory of his name. True, indeed, in the Papacy, God still retains his name, but as his glory is not comprehended in the mere letters of his name, it is certain that there he is not recognized as God. Know, therefore, that the true worship of God cannot be preserved in all its integrity until the base profanation of his glory, which is the inseparable attendant of superstition, be completely reformed.
